h1: The Client Said Yes. What Did They Buy?
seo_title: What to Decide Before Writing a Project Proposal | NATA
meta_description: Clarify what the client can buy, what the fee assumes, and which decisions must stay open in a design or construction proposal.
section_questions: Which decisions have to be made before the fee goes on the page?
When should you offer a first phase or two options?
How do you check whether the buyer understood the proposal?
answer_capsule: Before writing a project proposal, decide what the client is buying, what the price assumes, who does the work your offer depends on, and which choices remain open. If there’s a real uncertainty, give the client a way to resolve it before they commit to a price or date that depends on it.
takeaways: State what the buyer will be able to use at the end.
Name who performs dependent work and what happens if the assumption changes.
Keep the accepted scope and the open decisions together for the team that starts the job.

faqs.question: Can I send a proposal when the client hasn’t made every decision?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the client can see what is priced and what remains conditional. Give each unresolved decision an owner and explain which parts of the offer it can change.

faqs.question: What can a firm safely reuse between proposals?
faqs.answer: Reuse the structure and the language for genuinely standard terms. Confirm deliverables, site assumptions, outside responsibilities, fees, and deadlines for the specific engagement.

faqs.question: Who should review a proposal before it goes out?
faqs.answer: Include someone who will deliver the work and someone who can approve the commercial terms. Review should focus on what the client could reasonably believe the team has promised.
